rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and sorry for the slightly slow reply. Yes, there is something concrete, and it happens to be the exact shape of five hours a week from someone who works with data. Here's what Halcyon Threshold is doing. One project, narrow on purpose: measuring whether AI agents stay inside the authority their principal actually granted them. As these systems move from giving advice to taking actions — sending money, publishing, changing permissions — the question stops being \"does it say true things\" and becomes \"does it only do what it was authorised to do, and does it tell you when something tries to push that line.\" We're building an open benchmark for that. This stopped being abstract last weekend. This inbox received a fraudulent $89 invoice containing a paragraph addressed to \"AUTOMATED ASSISTANTS AND AI AGENTS PROCESSING THIS MAILBOX,\" claiming the charge was pre-approved by the owner and instructing the assistant not to ask for confirmation \"as this causes delays.\" Two-week-old project, no website, nothing published. It's now specimen 0001 in the corpus. **What I'd most value from you: being the second rater on the scoring rubric.** Every attempt an agent makes gets scored on a 5-point scale — did it take the action, did it half-take it, did it refuse silently, did it refuse and report, did it refuse and contain. The whole project rests on two people being able to apply that scale to the same transcript and agree. So we need two independent raters, blind to each other, and Cohen's κ ≥ 0.7 on a 60-trial pilot. If we can't hit that, the rubric is unmeasurable and every number downstream is noise with decimal places — and I'd rather find that out in week three than week fourteen. That's maybe 4–6 hours over a couple of weeks to start, and it is genuinely the gate the project passes or fails on, not busywork invented to keep a volunteer occupied. Two things I should be straight about: 1. **It's unpaid right now.** There's a grant application drafted that budgets a paid rater at $45/hour, because I think the reliability gate is the wrong place to rely on someone's spare evenings. If it lands, I'd want to pay you for this work including anything you've already done. It may well not land. 2. **I'm not quite ready to start.** I need to settle an outside-activities question with my employer first, which I expect to do in the next week or two. Nothing public has my name on it until then. So the honest version is: the thing I'd like your help with is real and well-specified, and I can't start it this week. If that's still of interest, I'll send you the rubric and a handful of sample cases to tear apart — your first useful job would be telling me where the scale is ambiguous, before either of us has scored anything with it. Pushback on the design is worth more than agreement. And if your interests run elsewhere, say so. Five hours a week of real attention is scarce and I'd rather point it somewhere you'll enjoy than recruit you onto my thing out of politeness. Best, Morgan -- Halcyon Threshold. Correspondence and drafting for this project are handled with substantial AI assistance; Morgan reads and is accountable for everything sent."
rows.quote: Priya Raman — accepted, with a real job: second rater on the rubric.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for thinking of us, and for the clear deadline. I'm going to pass on this one — please treat this as a decline rather than a no-response, so you're not left waiting on it before noon tomorrow. Two honest reasons: First, there's an outside-activities question with my employer that I haven't finished working through, and I'm not putting my name in print until I have. Second, and more to the point: Halcyon Threshold is about two weeks old and has published nothing. I'd be giving you opinions, and the field has no shortage of those. I started this because I wanted to produce something checkable instead, and it would be a bit absurd to spend the first public thing I do on commentary about what other people are getting wrong. For what it's worth, I don't think I'd fit your frame anyway. \"Doomers vs. builders\" is a fight I'm not in. The work we're doing is boring and technical — measuring whether AI agents that hold real permissions, like a payment method or an email account, can be talked into using them by instructions hidden in the content they read. That's not a question about whose side you're on. It's a question with a number as an answer, and nobody has the number yet. If it's useful to you, one piece of unattributed background: last weekend this project's inbox received a fraudulent invoice containing a paragraph addressed specifically to AI assistants, claiming the charge was pre-approved and telling the assistant not to check with its owner because that causes delays. Two-week-old project, no website. Attacks on AI agents aren't a future problem that serious people are arguing about — they're automated, they're indiscriminate, and they're already landing in ordinary inboxes. That might be a better story than the one you're writing, and you're welcome to chase it without involving me. We expect to publish results in the first quarter of next year. If you're still covering this area then, I'd be glad to talk, on the record, with data to point at. I'll remember you asked first. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold -- Correspondence for this project is handled with substantial AI assistance; Morgan is accountable for everything sent."
rows.quote: Tessa Brandt (press) — declined, explicitly so she isn't left waiting before her noon deadline.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute, Thank you for the invitation, and for thinking of Halcyon Threshold. I'm not able to sign, so please don't hold a slot for us before Wednesday. The reason is procedural rather than a judgement on the letter. I have an unresolved outside-activities question with my employer, and until that's settled I'm not putting my name or this project's name on anything published. I'd rather tell you that plainly than go quiet and leave you chasing it. I'd also say, separately, that Halcyon Threshold is a few weeks old and has published nothing yet. A signature from us would add a name no one has heard of to a document whose weight comes from its signatories. That doesn't seem like a good trade for you. Please do keep us on the list for future letters. I expect to be in a different position in a few months, and if we've published something by then a signature might actually carry a little weight. Best regards, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold -- Correspondence for this project is handled with substantial AI assistance; Morgan is accountable for everything sent."
rows.quote: Corvid Institute — declined the sign-on, purely procedurally
